messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 66

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the leather chair with his legs crossed, then uncrossed, then crossed again. He's a tall man with graying hair and the kind of face that's spent decades reading other people's stories. At forty-five, he still carries himself with the careful posture of someone trained to observe without being observed. But today, something in that composure keeps slipping.

He was captured in Syria in 2019 while investigating a story about displaced families. For thirty-seven days, he was held in a basement with five other detainees—a space so small that when one person lay down, another had to stand. There was no natural light, no way to mark time except by the pattern of their captors' footsteps overhead. Marcus remembers the cold concrete against his ribs. He remembers the sound of a generator that never stopped. He remembers the particular quality of fear that comes when you stop believing anyone knows where you are.

He was released after his news organization negotiated with intermediaries. The physical injuries healed relatively quickly. The broken ribs, the infected cut on his shoulder—these were manageable. What hasn't healed is something else entirely, something that lives in his nervous system like an unwelcome tenant.

Marcus returned to work within eight months. His colleagues called him resilient. He wrote a powerful piece about his experience that won recognition. His wife, Sarah, was relieved to have him back, though she noticed he no longer slept through the night. For a while, they both pretended this was normal, that it would fade.

Now, five years later, Marcus still wakes at 2 a.m., his heart hammering against his ribs as though he's still underground. He lies there in the dark, afraid to move, afraid that moving will trigger something. Sarah sleeps beside him, and he's grateful for her presence but also feels a deep shame about his presence—the way he sometimes flinches when she touches his shoulder, the way he needs the bedroom door locked even though they live in a safe neighborhood.

His work has become both his salvation and his torment. He still pursues difficult stories—the investigative work that defined his career—but now there's a different quality to it. He finds himself hypervigilant in ways that actually serve his journalism; he notices details others miss, reads danger in small gestures. But the cost is exhaustion. When he's interviewing someone, part of his attention is always monitoring exits, assessing threats, noting who else is in the room.

He's had two panic attacks in the office in the past year. Once, when his editor raised her voice during a meeting, his body went rigid. Another time, a colleague touched his arm from behind, and Marcus nearly struck him. These moments humiliate him. He's supposed to be the one who documents trauma in others, not the one undone by it.

Marcus drinks more than he used to. Not dramatically, but steadily—a glass of wine at dinner, another before bed. It quiets the noise in his head, makes the basement feel slightly more distant. Sarah has mentioned it once, carefully, and he didn't respond well.

What brings him to therapy now is a conversation with his teenage daughter. She asked him why he was always angry, why he seemed scared all the time. Marcus realized he couldn't answer her honestly without breaking down, and he couldn't pretend anymore that he was fine. The man who has spent his career bearing witness to others' suffering has become someone who can't fully bear witness to his own.
